#9612. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9611. How to Evaluate Snowflake Cortex Embedding Models for Enterprise Search

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

A company has 500,000 support tickets sitting in Snowflake. Years of troubleshooting notes, product defects, workarounds, resolutions, and occasional messages that just say "fixed after restart." Very helpful, thanks.

Someone wants an AI assistant that can search those tickets and suggest resolutions. The architecture looks straightforward. Take the documents, generate embeddings, store vectors, retrieve similar records, and let an LLM write the answer.

A few SQL queries later, you have a demo.

Then someone asks which embedding model you picked.

And there it is. We've designed an intelligent search system using the same decision-making process people use to buy televisions. Snowflake Cortex offers eight built-in text embedding models through AI_EMBED. Some produce 768-dimensional vectors, others 1,024. Some are English-focused. Others support multiple languages. Context windows vary considerably.

I've spent about eight years working with Snowflake, and one lesson from enterprise data engineering keeps showing up: the technically impressive option isn't necessarily the right one for your workload. Embedding models are no exception.

According to Snowflake's AI_EMBED documentation, the built-in text embedding lineup includes:

Snowflake also supports image embeddings through voyage-multimodal-3, but that's a different use case. We're keeping this investigation focused on text.

Eight models sound like eight chances to get it right. Or eight chances to explain to your architect why you chose one based on a name.

A 1,024-dimensional embedding contains more numbers than a 768-dimensional embedding. More numbers must mean more meaning. Unfortunately, vector search doesn't work like upgrading a laptop from 16 GB to 32 GB of RAM.

An embedding model learns a representation of language. Its dimensions are coordinates in that learned space, not a score for intelligence.

A larger representation might capture useful distinctions. It might also deliver no measurable improvement on your particular documents.

Imagine three fictional incident records:

"Why did settlement reconciliation fail after the column changed?"

A useful model should recognize that A and B are relevant, while C is mostly unrelated.

But here's the interesting part. Suppose a 768-dimensional model puts B first, while a 1,024-dimensional model puts A first.

You can't answer that from the dimension count. Maybe both are valid. Maybe one describes the exact failure while the other concerns an older version of the pipeline. Maybe neither contains the accepted resolution.

The model's job isn't to produce a beautiful vector.

For an English-only knowledge base containing relatively short documents, I'd start with a compact model such as Arctic Embed M v1.5 as a baseline.

Then I'd test whether a larger model improves retrieval.

Some tickets are in English. Others are in Spanish, French, Japanese, or a combination of languages.

"El proceso de conciliación falló después de modificar una columna."

"Why did reconciliation fail after the column update?"

Ideally, your retrieval system can connect these without requiring every ticket to be translated first. This is where models such as multilingual-e5-large, Arctic Embed L v2.0, and Voyage Multilingual 2 become candidates.

But multilingual support comes with an uncomfortable question. Does supporting multiple languages mean equally good retrieval in every language?

A model can support multilingual embeddings and still perform differently across languages, technical domains, and query styles.

An error such as ERR_RECON_042 should remain ERR_RECON_042, regardless of the surrounding language.

A model that understands a Spanish sentence but loses the exact error identifier hasn't solved the whole problem. I'd also separate two questions: can the model retrieve semantically similar information across languages, and does the retrieved information actually answer the user's question?

They're related, but they're not identical. Multilingual support earns a model a place in the evaluation. It doesn't automatically win the contract.

Consider a 40-page incident report. It contains the original failure, several failed fixes, the successful workaround, and a postmortem written two weeks later.

A model with a short context window can't embed the whole document in one pass. A model supporting longer inputs gives you more room.

Arctic Embed L v2.0 8K supports longer inputs than its standard version. Voyage Multilingual 2 supports up to 32,000 tokens. At first glance, longer sounds better. Fewer chunks. Less processing logic. Everybody goes home early.

That 40-page report isn't necessarily about one thing.

The first section describes ingestion. The second discusses schema evolution. The third explains a permissions issue. The fourth says the original root-cause theory was wrong. Put everything into one vector and you're asking the model to summarize several distinct concepts into a single location in embedding space.

Now imagine a user searching specifically for the permissions issue.

Will the document-level vector represent that section strongly enough? Maybe. But I wouldn't bet the retrieval architecture on it.

Chunking exists for a reason. Sometimes a focused 300-token chunk retrieves better than an entire document represented by one embedding. Sometimes larger context helps preserve the explanation that a smaller chunk would lose.

The answer depends on the structure of the content.

I'd compare different chunking strategies before spending time arguing about context-window sizes. The bigger window may be useful. It isn't permission to stop thinking about document structure.

One thing I like about the Cortex approach is that generating a text embedding doesn't require standing up a separate model-serving application.

Let's use a small fictional knowledge base.

For this illustrative example, we're calculating similarity against a tiny table. It's not a proposed production retrieval architecture for millions of documents.

More importantly, this SQL demonstrates how to retrieve candidates, not whether the chosen model retrieves the right candidates.

And no, I haven't run this example across all eight models and discovered a secret winner. There are no fabricated benchmarks hiding behind the curtain.

The goal here is to make the model-selection process understandable and reproducible.

Here's my favorite trap in semantic search.

The system retrieves a document discussing reconciliation errors.

The correct document contains ERR_RECON_042, but a different document talks about similar failures in more natural language. The embedding model prefers the descriptive document. Now the LLM receives the wrong evidence and writes a perfectly polished answer.

We've successfully automated being confidently incorrect.

This is why I wouldn't build enterprise retrieval around vector similarity alone. Exact identifiers, error codes, schema names, version numbers, and product IDs often deserve lexical matching. Semantic search helps when people describe the same problem differently. Keyword search helps when the exact characters matter. Both can be useful.

Cortex Search supports hybrid retrieval, making it worth evaluating for applications that need semantic and lexical matching together.

The right question isn't always "Which embedding model should I use?"

Sometimes it's "Why am I asking an embedding model to solve a problem that exact matching handles better?" A screwdriver isn't a bad tool because it struggles with nails.

Let's say you've embedded two million documents using snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5.

Six months later, a new model looks promising. Someone changes the model name used to generate query embeddings.

The stored documents were embedded with the old model. Your queries now use a different model. Even if two models return vectors with identical dimensions, their embedding spaces aren't necessarily compatible. And if one returns 768 dimensions while the other returns 1,024, the mismatch is even more obvious.

So switching models isn't just a configuration change.

You may need to regenerate embeddings for the corpus, maintain parallel indexes, measure retrieval changes, and coordinate the cutover.

This may sound like too much metadata for a vector. Until someone asks why search behavior changed last Tuesday. Then suddenly everyone loves metadata.

If I were evaluating embedding models for a real enterprise application, I wouldn't start with a leaderboard.

I'd start with a set of questions and known relevant documents. For an initial experiment, something like 100–200 representative queries could help expose failure patterns, although broader testing would be needed before making general performance claims.

I'd include straightforward questions, ambiguous queries, similar-but-wrong incidents, multilingual examples, and cases with no valid answer. Then I'd compare candidate models against the same data.

Did the correct evidence make the top five?

How high did the first relevant result appear?

Were the most relevant results ranked appropriately?

How quickly can the model process a search query?

What does it cost to embed the document collection?

How expensive is a future model migration?

What kinds of questions does the model get wrong?

I'd measure actual costs using Snowflake's current pricing and usage information rather than infer them from vector dimensions. And I'd pay special attention to the failures.

Suppose Model A retrieves the correct document for 94 out of 100 questions. Model B succeeds on 96.

A routine FAQ? Or an incident where retrieving an outdated fix could cause another production outage?

Raw accuracy alone doesn't tell you which failure matters more.

That's the problem with declaring winners before understanding the workload.

There's a practical issue worth mentioning. You can have unused Snowflake trial credits and still be blocked from calling certain Cortex embedding functions.

For example, a trial account may return an error indicating that an internal embedding function isn't available. That isn't proof that the SQL syntax is wrong or the requested model doesn't exist.

Account eligibility, regional availability, permissions, and service access all matter. Before writing a benchmark, verify that the account can actually invoke the candidate models. It's a small step that can save an afternoon of debugging the wrong thing.

After looking at the options, here's how I'd approach model selection.

And for every category, verify model availability, pricing, and restrictions in your Snowflake region.

This isn't a universal ranking. It's a shortlist of where I'd begin testing.

Snowflake Cortex makes generating embeddings easy. Choosing the right model is still your responsibility.

Eight models don't mean eight levels of intelligence. A larger vector doesn't guarantee a better match. A longer context window doesn't eliminate chunking. And multilingual support doesn't guarantee that every language or technical domain performs equally well.

A model can retrieve something semantically similar and still miss the evidence your application needs. That's the part worth testing.

If I had to make the decision tomorrow, I'd start with a simple baseline, build a representative evaluation set, and bring in more capable models only when they solve a measured problem.

Because the embedding model isn't supposed to win a beauty contest.

It's supposed to find the right document. And when it doesn't, I'd much rather know that before the LLM writes three paragraphs explaining the wrong answer.

Author’s note: The scenarios and SQL examples in this article are illustrative. They are not drawn from confidential systems, and no comparative benchmark results are claimed.

#9610. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9607. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9605. How to Watch the Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order

Entertainment writer. Loves games, movies, and comics. Also loves talking in the third person

Entertainment writer. Loves games, movies, and comics. Also loves talking in the third person

Entertainment writer. Loves games, movies, and comics. Also loves talking in the third person

So, full disclosure, I don’t really believe in watching movies in chronological order the first time around. I think that watching them by release date is usually the best way to go. However, if you’re planning on doing it for the Hunger Games movies, I’ve got you covered. Here are all the Hunger Games movies in chronological order.

The first movie in the Hunger Games’ timeline, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes sees a young Coriolanus Snow trying to navigate the craziness that is the country of Panem. He eventually finds himself actively involved in the 10th annual Hunger Games as a mentor for District 12’s female tribute, Lucy Gray Baird.

Snow wants to be on top of the world, which means he’ll do anything and everything to see his dream realized. Cheat, kill, backstab - nothing is off limits if it means inching closer and closer to the top.

Set 40 years after the events of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, it focuses on District 12 male tribute Haymitch Abernathy as he is forced to compete in the 50th Hunger Games. This time, though, the rules have changed. Every 25th Hunger Games, a new concept is added to make that year’s game even more special.

So, for the 50th Hunger Games, they decide to double the number of tributes. 48 in total, 4 from each district. It’s hard enough to win a normal Hunger Games, but to do it with double the people is damn near impossible. Haymitch will have to overcome the overwhelming odds if he wants to survive.

Fast forward 24 years, and we arrive at the 74th Hunger Games. Yes, the Hunger Games are still going, but the 12 Districts that are forced to send their children to death every year are sick and tired of it all. Revolution is coming. All it needs is for someone to light the fire.

In the midst of all this, District 12 teenager Katniss Everdeen volunteers to participate in the Hunger Games in place of her little sister. Alongside District 12 male tribute Peeta Mellark, Katniss will have to train and learn the inner workings of the games to outlast the other tributes and make it back home to her family.

The fire of rebellion is spreading, and the government of Panem knows that it has to do something before it spreads too far. Katniss, who survived last year’s games, is seen as a dangerous individual who’s fanning the flames. President Snow decides that something has to be done about her and the other former Hunger Games victors.

For the 75th Hunger Games, a new special concept is added. Katniss and 23 other former Hunger Games winners will return to compete to the death. Knowing that they’re beloved by the populace, they tug at their heartstrings to try and get out of the games, further pushing people to revolt.

The rebellion is in full swing following the games, and Katniss, whether she wants to or not, is seen as the face of it. Most of the districts are quick to join her side, but President Snow won’t go quietly into that good night. He still has a few tricks up his sleeve, including brainwashing someone who’s very close to Katniss. I can’t go into more detail without spoiling the movie, but this is where things get serious. And they only get more serious in the following and final movie.

The war between the rebellion and President Snow is finally coming to an end. All the districts are united against him; the only thing left to do is to storm the Capitol and to take down the president himself. But President Snow refuses to lose gracefully. Throughout the city, he has laid out traps for Katniss and her team. They’ll have to do their best to avoid these dangerous pods and make it to Snow’s mansion in one piece.

The Hunger Games are often lumped with other YA novel adaptations from that era, but I think that this film series is far and away one of the best in its genre. If you’re watching these movies for the first time, I encourage you to do it by release date. However, if you think it best to go by timeline order, I hope this Hunger Games in chronological order list serves you well.

#9603. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

#9602. Ship it reversible: designing the undo layer an agent's irreversible actions need

The worst minute of operating an assistant was not a hallucination. It was a cheerful confirmation: "Done — I cancelled the appointment and sent the shop a note explaining why."

The appointment was gone. The note was in a stranger's inbox. Neither of those is a state I can put back. There is no ctrl+z for a message someone has already read, and no version of "cancel" that returns the slot the shop had already re-let.

I build an assistant that runs errands in the real world: forms, checkouts, bookings, cancellations, mail. Every design review I have with myself ends up in the same place. The interesting question is not can the agent do it. It is what does it cost to take it back, and who gets to find out.

We talk about "safe actions" as if safety lived in the API call. It does not. The same delete is a non-event on a draft and a catastrophe on the only copy of a tax document. Four things decide the class, and only one of them is in the code:

I now tag every effect with one of four classes before it runs:

The classification takes ten minutes and changes the architecture. The agent stops treating "done" as one word.

Reversibility is not a boolean you find; it is something you manufacture. Five dials, in the order I reach for them.

1. Delay. Put the effect in a queue with a countdown instead of executing it. Forty seconds is enough for the person to read the confirmation line and say stop, and cheap enough that nothing else in the system notices. A delay is only honest if the countdown is visible and the item can still be withdrawn at second 39.

2. Snapshot. Before any destructive write, read the current value and store it with the effect record — not the new value, the old one. prior_state is the single field that turns most R-class mistakes into a non-event, and it is the field everybody forgets, because the happy path never reads it.

3. Stage. Split the action into a state that nobody minds and a promotion that everybody minds. A draft in the same mailbox the send would use; a preview URL that renders exactly the live page; a status='staged' row that a human or a second check promotes. Two-phase publish costs one extra state and one extra write, and it is the difference between "I posted the wrong thing" and "I staged the wrong thing".

4. Trash instead of delete. Delete sets deleted_at and hides the row; a nightly job removes it after thirty days. A tombstone is also a correct answer to "did this exist?" — which matters more than people expect when a later step needs to prove it acted on the right record.

5. Compensate. When none of the above applies, define the inverse explicitly and treat it as a first-class effect with its own record, its own approval and its own failure modes. A refund is not the absence of a charge.

Most real errands need two or three of these at once: a charge with a snapshot of the prior balance, behind a delay, with a refund path defined before the charge is allowed.

An "undo" button is a view over a record. If the record is thin, the button lies. Minimum shape:

Three of these fields do the real work. window_until makes the undo promise finite and therefore checkable. observed_by records the moment the effect stopped being private — the earliest point at which the inverse changes meaning. supersedes is the fence: an undo that arrives after the target has moved on is not an undo, it is a new decision.

Without status, an undo that failed looks identical to one that succeeded, and the next attempt is a guess.

This was the insight that changed how I set delays. The technical send is a write; the human event is delivery. Between those two is a variable-size gap I can use.

Practical rule: the hold window must end before any second party could plausibly observe the effect. For mail, that is a matter of seconds once it leaves your provider. For a booking, it is the moment the shop's calendar re-let the slot. For a public post, it is the first crawl or the first read. For a phone call, it is the first word spoken — which is why I treat outbound calls as X-class by default and require a person to be the one who places them.

Two corollaries I had to learn by breaking things:

A confirmation dialog is the cheapest possible reversibility, and the weakest: it moves the cost to the person's attention, once per action, forever. Downgrading the action removes the risk structurally. The table I keep, roughly:

Note the last row. When a site has no draft, the reversible substitute is a read-back: extract what will be submitted, compare it to what was intended, and only then press the button. It is not an undo, but it catches the majority of wrong-field errors before they become X-class.

This is where I see the most confident mistakes. An inverse is a new effect with its own consequences:

So compensation follows the same gate as any other C-class action: it needs its terms stated, a window, and — for anything a stranger will read — a drafted text that a human releases. An automated apology is how a small slip becomes a public incident.

The inverse is a tool call, so it inherits every tool-call problem: unknown outcomes, retries, duplicates. Three tests catch almost all of it.

Twice. Undo must be idempotent against its own record. status moves applied → undone once; the second call reads undone and returns it instead of running the inverse again. Without this, an undo that timed out and was retried re-books the slot that the first undo already released.

Late. After window_until, the inverse is refused and the refusal is reported, not silently downgraded. A promise you cannot keep is worse than a promise you never made; the person is planning around the sentence you printed.

After the world moved. Compare the target's current state to prior_state. If it differs in the fields the inverse assumes — the row was edited, the slot was re-let, the person replied — the undo is superseded, and the right output is a question, not an action. This is the same fence that stops a stale background job from writing, applied to the reverse direction.

I also test the dependency case, which is the one that hits hardest: effect A was undone while effect B was derived from it. A calendar invite derived from a cancelled booking, a receipt derived from a refunded charge. The rule I settled on is that derived effects carry the id of their cause, and undoing a cause marks its dependants orphaned for review rather than deleting them. An orphan list is a queue of questions; a silent cascade is a second incident.

The tests that paid for themselves, all run against a scratch account:

Test 7 is the one that turns a demo into an operating system. Most undo buttons I have used are only tested for the happy path, so the interesting states — half-undone, compensation failed, orphaned dependants — are exactly the states nobody has ever seen.

Reversibility is a promise made in the interface, so it has to be legible before the decision:

And the agent should be able to say the uncomfortable sentence: "I already did the part that cannot be undone; here is what I can still do." That sentence is more useful than any success message, and it is the sentence an agent can only produce if the record told the truth about observed_by.

If the X-class undo rate is above zero, the fix is upstream: downgrade the action so it stops being X-class. Undo exists to cover the residual, not to make irreversible actions acceptable.

None of this makes an agent trustworthy. It makes its mistakes priced in advance — and it means the one action nobody can take back is the one the agent was never allowed to take quietly.

If you want the phone-side version of these mechanics — what a daily usage limit does, what a reset ticket restores, where the irreversible boundary sits in a consumer assistant — I keep two public notes:

Disclosure: I use Pickle, a phone-side AI assistant app, and I am not its vendor. The two links above are mine; if a sign-up completes through the invite link, both sides receive reset tickets, and the app's own notices govern any benefit. This is not a paid placement. The reversibility model described here is the one I run in my own errand-running agent, written from mistakes I made on live accounts.

#9599. ESPHome Body Matches Mostly Describe Documentation and Devices

ESPHome firmware can expose a small web server for monitoring and control, and its project documentation is widely indexed. Those two facts explain why a body count can dwarf an application fingerprint. On November 15, 2026, ZoomEye returned zero matches for app="ESPHome", 839 for title="ESPHome" and 830,661 for http.body="ESPHome" with sub_type=all, page 1 and page size 1.

The 830,661 body matches are not 830,661 exposed devices. The string appears in documentation, tutorials, package pages, configuration examples and firmware-generated content. The title count is narrower but still includes docs and unrelated projects. The zero app count means this field did not classify the product in the run; it does not prove that no ESPHome deployment exists.

ESPHome's web server documentation says authentication is optional and recommends always setting a password when the server is enabled. Device security also depends on the native API, OTA update path and network placement. A reachable dashboard can control relays, sensors or other physical functions. A firmware update endpoint can change the device's behavior. These are different authorities even though both may be served by the same device.

Inventory owned devices by hostname, firmware version, configuration source, network segment and enabled services. Verify that the web server has authentication if it is enabled, that OTA is restricted to trusted networks, and that the device cannot reach arbitrary internet destinations. Store Wi-Fi and API secrets in the configuration's secret mechanism rather than in a public repository.

The review should distinguish a device's web page from the ESPHome dashboard used to build firmware. They are separate services with separate credentials and update authority. Do not scan public addresses outside an authorized scope just because a body query returns a large number.

For owned assets, test an unauthenticated read, an unauthenticated control action, and an OTA attempt from outside the approved network. Keep the device on a segmented network and log configuration changes. The count is useful for finding product references, but the security decision belongs to the device's physical and network owner.

#9598. How I Built an AI Marketing Team With Grok Bot Without Writing Code

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Sam Brovda (Samuel Brovda) comes from the sales world and builds software on the side with AI coding agents.

Last time I wrote about building a consumer mobile app on nights and weekends with AI coding agents.

The code was only half the problem. An app nobody hears about is a hobby. And I don’t have a marketing team.

So I built one out of bots. I use Grok Bot, where each bot has its own computer and can run jobs on a schedule. Here’s how it’s set up and what I’ve learned so far.

My first instinct was one big assistant that does everything. That’s like hiring one rep to prospect, run demos, do legal, and forecast. Nothing gets done well.

So every bot gets one job, written at the top of its instructions.

That last list matters more than the job itself. It’s the same lesson from coding agents. An agent with no boundaries will happily do things you never asked for.

The marketing bot never posts, comments, or messages anyone. It drafts. I post.

That one rule removes most of the risk. A bad draft costs me thirty seconds. A bad post under my name costs a lot more.

It’s approval tiers again. A rep can draft the proposal. They can’t sign the contract.

The marketing bot has one rules file, and every job reads it before doing anything. It holds the guardrails and a lessons section.

Then once a week, the Friday report adds a few plain lessons to the bottom. These are real ones from the first week:

Then I changed the goal. Since there’s no signup page, posts stopped asking people to sign up. Now they close on a follow or a comment prompt. The bot wrote that change into the same file, with the date, so every job picks it up the next morning.

If you read my last piece, this will sound familiar. It’s the same idea as the instruction file for my coding agent. If a decision only lives in a chat, the next run won’t know about it.

Early on, the marketing bot built a content bank: 21 days of posts, planned out, so I’m never starting from a blank page.

That’s the real win for me. Not that the bot is creative. That I don’t have to decide what to post every single day. I review a plan, say yes or no, and move on.

Bots drift. They’ll report “done” on things that half-happened.

So the chief of staff bot doesn’t trust the reports. It reads the actual output. If a bot is off track, it nudges that bot once with the goal, what’s missing, and the next step. If it’s still off the next day, it flags it to me.

Its rules say never invent progress or metrics, and mark anything it can’t verify as unverified. I want a pipeline review, not a happy-ears forecast.

You don’t need a marketing team to start. You need a few narrow bots and a way to catch them when they’re wrong.

For me that’s four things. One job per bot. A list of things each bot must never do. A rules file that collects lessons with dates. And nothing goes out under my name without my yes.

Even this post works that way. A bot drafted it from the work we actually did, and it doesn’t go up until I approve it.

I’m Sam Brovda. I come from enterprise sales and write about building software as a non-engineer.

#9595. Who actually arrived: telling a reader, a crawler, and your own robot apart in one event table

You ship a small page. You add a counter. A week later the counter says thirteen visitors, and you start making decisions from it — this copy works, that aggregator sends traffic, the landing page is worth improving.

Then you look at the rows and find that four of the thirteen were not people at all. Two were your own deploy check. One was a crawler. One was a link-preview bot from a chat app, fetching your title so a stranger could see a card. You did not lose the visitors; you never had them. The number was never a count of people. It was a count of requests, and requests are made by programs.

This article is about the small event table that fixes that, the classification ladder that makes its numbers defensible, and the specific ways those numbers lie even after you build it properly. It is written for the case most solo builders are actually in: no analytics vendor, no consent banner, one table you control, and a need to answer "did anyone come, and did they do anything" without fooling yourself.

Start with the honest description of the data. Each row records that something fetched a URL at a time, with a referrer it claimed, from an address your server saw, with a user agent it volunteered. Everything about a person is inference on top of that.

So the table should hold what you can defend, and nothing that pretends to know more:

Do not delete your own traffic; flag it. Internal rows are the audit trail that your deploy, your check script and your monitoring all still work. Delete them and the next time the counter reads zero you cannot tell whether the page is fine or the instrumentation died. Keep the row, exclude it by is_internal = 0 in every query, and require a reason string so a later you can disagree with the classification.

The temptation is a single boolean, is_bot. That boolean will be wrong in both directions: it will mark a curious reader who pastes a link into a terminal as a robot, and it will let a headless browser through because it had no user agent at all.

Use an ordered ladder instead, first match wins:

And then the naming discipline that matters more than the ladder: the last bucket is "not identified as a robot", not "human". Report it that way. A number labelled honestly is still useful; a number labelled wishfully gets built on.

The reason strings are the part that pays off months later. When you reclassify, you reclassify by reason, not by guessing which rows were which:

Every deploy you open the page to see whether the stylesheet loaded. Every check script you will write over the next month (see the companion piece on schedules and checks) touches the same route. Left alone, that is a steady drip of "visitors" that scales with how much you work — which is precisely backwards, because the busiest weeks look like the most successful ones.

The failure mode to plan against: an internal exclusion that quietly catches real people. That happens when the rule is broad — "user agent contains curl" — and someone genuinely arrives from a terminal. The reason string is what saves you: when the totals look wrong, sort by reason and read the rows.

A user agent is self-reported and trivially forgeable, so it is evidence, never proof. What a crawler actually looks like in an event table is a shape, and the shape is more reliable than the string:

Reverse DNS is not the answer either — it is slow, frequently absent, and still spoofable in the direction that matters. If you need proof, verify that a claimed crawler address belongs to the crawler's published ranges, and cache the result. Otherwise accept that you are estimating, and keep the reason string so the estimate is auditable.

There is one more crawler class worth its own bucket because it confuses funnel math: the preview fetcher. When someone shares your link in a chat app, the app fetches the page to render a card. That request is a real request, sometimes from a real person's account, and it produces a view with no click, no scroll, and no second request. If your page's job is to get someone to press a button, a preview fetch is a false positive on the first funnel step, and it arrives exactly when you have shared the link somewhere — which is when you are most eager to read the numbers.

Two habits make "nothing happened" a claim instead of a guess.

Measure twice: at the start and the end of the work. A job that reads the table at 06:54 and reports "zero new" is making a statement about a window it never defined. Read again at 07:01, and now the statement is: from row 687 to row 687, over the interval between two timestamps. Nine quiet minutes. That is a fact, and it is falsifiable.

This is not pedantry. Events land between runs. A visitor who arrives two minutes after one run's last read and before the next run's scheduled time is invisible to both the "no traffic" report and the "we had traffic" report, and you will spend an afternoon trying to explain why a channel appears to do nothing while the totals keep growing:

Watermark by id, not by timestamp. WHERE created_at > last_seen skips rows that share a second with the watermark — and in a burst, several rows do. Ids from a monotonically increasing sequence give you an exact, tie-free boundary. If you do not have one, take the timestamp as a boundary and the max id at that timestamp.

Store UTC; display local. One field, one timezone, converted at the edge. The alternative is a database whose meaning depends on which report you are reading, and a bug you will find at the worst possible hour.

You will have days that look like this: thirteen view rows, two click rows. The arithmetic that leaps to mind is 15.4%, and it is worse than useless — it invites a decision about copy from a sample where one more click would move the number eight points.

The rule I use: report counts until n is large enough to make a rate meaningful, and always name the denominator. "Two clicks from thirteen arrivals, over 24 hours, two of the arrivals on different days" is honest. "15% click-through" implies a stability the data does not have.

The same caution applies to deduplication. Counting rows counts events; counting distinct ip_hash counts something like sessions. They answer different questions, and the gap between them is information: thirteen rows from thirteen hashes is thirteen separate arrivals; thirteen rows from three hashes is one enthusiast and a refresh button. Choose deliberately, and print both.

The referrer header is the only free signal that says how someone arrived, and browsers strip it constantly: cross-origin navigation without a referrer policy, links opened from apps, and anything typed or pasted. So a blank referrer is not "direct traffic". It is "unknown", and labelling it "direct" in a report is how people conclude that their search traffic is worthless.

What the referrer is good for is chains. If your link is listed on an aggregator page, and that page links to three of your routes, you will see a recognisable shape:

And when a path has views but the next step in the funnel has never a single row from any referrer, that is a finding of its own — though not the finding you want. It can be a copy problem (nobody wanted to press it) or an instrumentation problem (the button's event never fires). The table alone cannot tell you which; you find out by being one of the arrivals and checking that your own click produced a row.

That check — do my own events appear, and with the shape I expect — is worth running after every change to the page. An event table nobody has verified against their own behaviour is a table of wishes.

Three things people expect an event table to answer, which it does not:

The one addition that pays for itself: the same classification on the downstream event as on the arrival, so the funnel's steps are computed over the same population. If arrivals exclude robots and clicks do not, your conversion rate silently includes robots clicking.

Aggregating early feels tidy and is a one-way door. Daily rollups answer "how many on Tuesday" and cannot answer "did the arrivals from that listing click", which is the question you will actually have in three weeks.

Keep raw rows long enough to cover the questions you can currently imagine asking — a few months for a personal project — then roll up to daily counts by path, event, referrer class, plus the distinct-person count. Aggregate by reason as well as flag, so a later reclassification does not require the raw rows you just deleted.

None of this makes the table correct. It makes it auditable — which is the only property that matters, because the moment you trust a number you cannot explain, you have stopped measuring and started guessing with extra steps.

Disclosure: I build and write about small automation tools, and I run an English guide for an AI assistant app whose invite system I use as a working example of these ideas: Pickle invite code SY3LC2 — how to enter it and the invite link pickle.com/i/RDKXK77G9ZRT. If someone joins through that link, I receive in-app usage credit; it costs the person joining nothing. Nothing in the article depends on that product, and the analytics design described is generic.

#9594. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.
