#9592. Gemini 4 or Gemma 4? It Depends.

This article provides a step by step guide to comparing the new Gemini 4 models with Gemma 4 on equal terms. Seven models, Gemma 4 26B and 31B, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.8 Flash, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon, run through the same Gemini API endpoint with the same questions, settings and scoring, started at the same moment.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/gemini-api-google-hydrogen4

The scores: on 1,319 GSM8K math problems Argon scored 0.9841, Hydrogen and Carbon 0.9803, 3.8 Flash 0.9788, Gemma 4 26B 0.9742, Gemma 4 31B 0.9735 and 3.5 Flash-Lite 0.9629. On 400 BFCL function calls Argon and Gemma 4 31B tied at 0.9675. Gemma 4 ran free; the Gemini runs cost $0.92 to $5.02. Hydrogen answered fastest of the Gemini 4 models, 2.84 s per GSM8K problem against 7.63 s for Argon.

The surprise is in the cost, and it takes the whole picture to see it. Hydrogen is the cheapest Gemini 4 model per token, $7.50 per million output tokens against $10 for Carbon and Argon, and it cost the most per run, $5.02 against $3.46 for Argon. Its thinking eats the token budget: Google's docs say reasoning cannot be turned off on Gemini 4 models, it ran on all 1,319 GSM8K problems at the lowest setting, and it was 55% of the GSM8K bill. Price per token, tokens per answer and thinking per answer together set what a model costs.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon are on the Gemini API next to the 3.x Flash models and Gemma 4. Google's pricing page, saved on 2026-11-14 (paid tier, USD per million tokens; output includes thinking tokens):

Carbon and Argon go to $4 / $20 on 2026-12-01, and 3.8 Flash to $1.50 / $7.50 on 2027-01-01.

Step 2 shows that setting for each model, and the two models that keep thinking at it.

The Gemini API answers OpenAI chat requests with the key as a Bearer token. Gemma 4 and Gemini take the same request body; only model changes:

The OpenAI endpoint sets thinking with reasoning_effort. levels.sh sends the question to every model with each value:

Gemma 4 and Flash-Lite go down to minimal, and there they think zero tokens. Hydrogen, 3.8 Flash, Carbon and Argon go down to none; Carbon and Argon think zero tokens there, and Hydrogen and 3.8 Flash keep thinking.

Google documents this. Its OpenAI compatibility page says "Reasoning cannot be turned off for Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3, or Gemini 4 models", and its thinking page lists Hydrogen's levels as low, medium, high and xhigh, with minimal "Not supported on Gemini 4 models or gemini-3.8-flash". The same page documents none for 2.5 models only. On Hydrogen, 3.8 Flash, Carbon and Argon the endpoint accepts none and treats it as low. On the first 100 GSM8K problems (levels-sample/), thinking tokens per problem:

So this run's none is each model's lowest documented level, low. The native API's other controls give the same result on the test question. thinking-controls.sh tries each on Hydrogen and reads the API's own counter, thoughtsTokenCount:

With thinkingBudget: 0 and includeThoughts: true, the reply carries the thought itself, beginning "Okay, here's my breakdown of this little egg scenario". 3.8 Flash reports 74 thinking tokens on that question under every control.

Across the full run, Hydrogen thought on 1,319 of 1,319 GSM8K problems and all 400 BFCL calls. 3.8 Flash thought on 1,293 GSM8K problems and 113 BFCL calls, Carbon on 268 GSM8K problems, Argon on 66, and Gemma 4 and Flash-Lite on none. Every one of those tokens is billed as output. Hydrogen also thought on "Say hi." (more-checks.sh).

On this endpoint completion_tokens counts only the visible answer. Thinking is total_tokens - prompt_tokens - completion_tokens, and Google bills it as output. The scoring script records it as reasoning_tokens on every row.

gemma4-dev names a rig ---. On the Gemini API the platform is gemini, the runtime api and the hardware google, since Google publishes neither; the model slot is the Gemma size or the Gemini family:

Each tpu.env names the model and the lowest thinking value it accepts, and the seven run.sh files are identical:

jev-tpu-v5e1/gen_eval.py scores every Gemma 4 rig in the repo. GSM8K is right when the number after Answer: matches; BFCL simple is right when the one function call passes BFCL's own checks. Four settings point it at a hosted API:

Three Gemma 4 requests hit the free tier's rate limit (HTTP 429) after every retry. resend_errors.py sent those three again with the same settings and replaced only those rows; all three came back right. Every answer in the table below is a model answer.

derived.py builds the table from the saved replies. The cost is the token counts the API returned times the list price.

Against Gemma 4 31B on the same questions, counting the questions each got right that the other missed:

Ahead and behind mean the 95% range of the difference, from 2,000 resamples of the questions, sits entirely above or below zero.

By list price Hydrogen is the cheapest Gemini 4 model, $7.50 per million output tokens against $10 for Carbon and Argon. It cost the most because it thought on all 1,319 GSM8K problems at its lowest setting, 248.7 thinking tokens each on average, which made thinking 55% of its GSM8K bill, against 11% for Carbon and 2% for Argon. Argon thought on 66 problems and scored the highest.

The Gemini 4 models also count more input tokens for the same text: the GSM8K prompts are 160,432 tokens to Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon and 120,902 to Gemma 4 31B, Flash-Lite and 3.8 Flash, a mean of 121.6 against 91.7 per problem.

Thinking also shares the output limit with the answer. Google's Hydrogen page says max_output_tokens "caps combined thinking and output tokens". At this run's limits of 2,048 and 512 tokens, thinking used the limit before the answer arrived on 4 GSM8K problems and 2 BFCL calls for 3.8 Flash and on 5 GSM8K problems for Carbon; all 11 scored wrong. Sent again with a 16,384-token limit (cut-rows.py), 2 of the 4 on 3.8 Flash and 3 of the 5 on Carbon came back right. Hydrogen had no cut answers.

Each reply records how long its request took. All seven models ran at once, eight requests at a time each, over the same connection, so the times are comparable with each other on that morning:

Hydrogen writes about 147.8 tokens per second per request, thinking included, against 26.1 for Argon and 29.7 for Carbon. It finished GSM8K in about a third of Argon's time while thinking on every problem. Flash-Lite was the fastest model overall.

Google documents both facts behind Hydrogen's bill: reasoning cannot be turned off on Gemini 4 models, and output prices include thinking tokens. Four things in the API still make the bill easy to misread:

Compare models by cost per answer, measured on your own prompts.

For the best scores on short math problems and single function calls with thinking at its lowest setting, Gemini 4 Argon: highest on GSM8K, tied for highest on BFCL, and the cheapest of the three Gemini 4 models per run because it rarely thinks.

For hard, multi-step work, Google points to Carbon. Its Hydrogen page calls Carbon "our strongest frontier model", one that "spends more thinking tokens per turn to test hypotheses and verify edge cases on hard architecture, debugging, science, and security audits", and suggests pairing the two: Carbon plans and resolves hard roadblocks, Hydrogen does the code edits, subagent tasks and test runs. This run held Carbon to its lowest thinking setting, where it thought on 268 of 1,319 GSM8K problems, so that case is untested here. Five of its GSM8K answers were cut at the 2,048-token limit; with a 16,384-token limit 3 of them came back right, which still leaves it below Argon.

For high-volume simple work on a paid tier, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: $0.92 for both tests, no thinking, 1.10 s per problem, at the cost of being behind Gemma 4 31B on both tests.

For tool calling at no cost, Gemma 4 31B: tied with Argon on BFCL, 0.0106 behind it on GSM8K, free on the Gemini API, and the same weights run on your own hardware.

The goal of this article was to compare the new Gemini 4 models with Gemma 4 on equal terms. The key to the solution was running all seven models through one Gemini API endpoint, started together, with the same questions, scoring script and settings, with thinking set as low as each model accepts. The results were:

Scope: one laptop in the US calling the Gemini API on 2026-11-14, one run per model, all seven started together. Thinking was set as low as each model accepts: minimal for Gemma 4 and Flash-Lite, none for the rest, which matched low on a 100-problem sample. The native thinking controls were tried on one question. The scores for 3.8 Flash and Carbon include the 11 answers cut by thinking at the 2,048 and 512 token limits. Three Gemma 4 requests that hit the free tier's rate limit were sent again with the same settings. Costs are token counts times list prices. Run times are from one run with all seven sharing one connection, and will move with load on the service. Hard multi-step tasks and higher thinking levels were not measured, which is the work Google positions Carbon for. Google does not say what hardware or engine serves any of these models.

The strategy for comparing Gemini and Gemma 4 on equal terms was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

#9591. Shadow AI in the Workplace: Data Security Risks and Governance Strategies

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

A junior associate is sitting at their desk, trying to finish a 110-page agreement that has to be ready by 8:00 AM. The coffee has gone cold. After hours of reading the same pages, even simple clauses are becoming difficult to understand.

There is still a lot of work left, and very little time.

The associate opens a free AI chatbot on a personal phone and copies three clauses from the agreement. Within seconds, the tool provides a short summary. The work becomes a little easier, and the associate moves on to the next task.

But there is one problem. The law firm has already banned the use of public AI tools. Its computers block access to these websites, and employees have been warned not to use them for professional work. Yet the associate has found another way to access the same tool through a personal device.

The firm's system may show that its restrictions are working. But it cannot necessarily show what the associate has shared through a personal connection.

This is one way Shadow AI can enter a workplace. The employee may not intend to expose confidential information. They may simply be trying to finish an urgent task. But the information has still moved outside the organisation's control. And this raises a question that companies need to consider: If employees are still finding ways to use AI despite a workplace ban, is blocking access really enough to protect the organisation?

Shadow AI refers to the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without the knowledge or approval of their organisation. These tools may include public chatbots, AI writing assistants, browser extensions, coding tools and meeting transcription applications.

The problem is not limited to which tool an employee uses. It is also about what information they share with it.

An employee may upload a client document to get a summary, enter company data to prepare a report, or share a section of source code to find an error. These actions may appear harmless from the employee's point of view. However, the organisation may have no clear understanding of where that information goes, how it is stored or what happens to it after the task is completed.

Many companies have responded by restricting or blocking public AI platforms. Their concerns are understandable. Confidential information, customer records and business documents should not be shared with services that have not been properly assessed.

However, a restriction does not automatically change employee behaviour. If a company blocks an AI website but continues to expect employees to complete the same workload within the same deadlines, the reason for using AI does not disappear. Some employees may simply find another way to access it.

This is where the real problem begins. A company may successfully block an application on its office network while remaining unaware that employees are using the same application through personal phones, private accounts or other connections.

Banning AI may restrict access through official systems, but it does not necessarily stop its use. In some situations, it can move that use beyond the organisation's visibility.

The use of AI at work is growing faster than many organisations can introduce their own systems and policies.

Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index reported that 75% of global knowledge workers were using AI at work. Among those using AI, 78% were bringing their own AI tools to work, commonly described as Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI).

This pattern aligns with broader enterprise trends. Research from Gartner shows that over 41% of employees actively acquire, modify, or use technology outside the visibility of IT department.

These figures are important because they show that employees are not waiting for their organisations to introduce every tool they want to use. But they should be understood carefully: they show workplace AI adoption and the use of personal tools; they do not prove that corporate bans are the reason employees use them.

The reasons can be practical. A legal associate may want to understand a long agreement more quickly. A researcher may need to organise a large amount of information. A software engineer may want help finding an error in code. An employee preparing a presentation may use AI to create an initial draft.

In each case, the employee is trying to save time or complete a task more efficiently.

This does not make every use acceptable. Employees still have a responsibility to follow workplace policies and protect confidential information. But organisations also need to understand why employees are turning to tools that have not been approved.

A policy that only says "do not use AI" may not answer the questions employees face every day: Which tools can I use? What information can I share? What should I do when the approved system cannot handle my task?

When these questions remain unanswered, employees may make their own decisions. That is how a technology policy can become disconnected from actual workplace behaviour.

In April 2023, Samsung Electronics reportedly faced incidents in which employees entered sensitive internal information into ChatGPT. Reports described employees sharing semiconductor source code and internal meeting information while using the tool for work-related tasks.

The incident became an important warning for companies considering the use of public AI platforms. It showed that sensitive information can leave an organisation through an ordinary workplace activity. An employee does not need to hack a system or deliberately attack a company. Copying information into an external chatbot can itself create a serious exposure.

Samsung's response included restrictions on generative AI use. The incident demonstrates why companies became concerned about employees using public AI tools. It does not, by itself, prove that bans push employees towards personal devices. That is a separate issue that organisations need to examine through evidence about employee behaviour.

There is another important point here. When information is entered into an external AI service, the organisation needs to understand the service's data practices.

Different AI providers have different terms and settings. Some services may use submitted content for model improvement under certain conditions, while others offer business arrangements with different data-retention and training terms. It would be incorrect to assume that every public AI service handles every prompt in the same way.

The concern is that employees using personal accounts may not know which terms apply to their information. The organisation may also have no contract, security review or clear process through which it can manage that risk.

For companies and legal institutions, Shadow AI is not just an IT concern. It can affect confidential information, legal responsibilities, customer trust and business interests.

1.⁠ ⁠Confidentiality and Attorney-Client Privilege

Legal professionals regularly work with sensitive information. This includes client communications, draft agreements, litigation strategies, personal records and documents that have not been made public.

Uploading such material to an external AI service without proper approval can create serious confidentiality concerns.

However, it is important to distinguish confidentiality from attorney-client privilege. Sharing privileged information with a third-party service does not automatically waive privilege in every situation. The legal result depends on the jurisdiction, the circumstances of disclosure, the service provider's access and the steps taken to maintain confidentiality.

Even where privilege is not automatically lost, sharing client information without proper safeguards may raise professional, contractual or ethical concerns.

For a law firm, the question should therefore not be limited to whether an AI tool gives a useful answer. It should also ask whether the information being shared is permitted to leave the firm's controlled environment.

2.⁠ ⁠Data Protection and Financial Penalties

The risk becomes more serious when employees share personal information through unapproved AI tools.

For example, a document may contain a client's name, address, financial details, identification information or other personal data. If that information is sent to an external service without appropriate safeguards, the organisation may face data-protection questions.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for penalties for specified failures. Under its Schedule, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore. This does not mean that every employee's use of an AI chatbot automatically leads to that penalty. The relevant legal duties, facts and circumstances must be considered.

Similarly, under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), certain serious infringements can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

These figures show why organisations need to take the handling of personal information seriously. But financial penalties are only one part of the problem. A data incident can also affect customer confidence, business relationships and the organisation's reputation.

IBM's 2023 Cost of a Data Breach Report estimated the global average cost of a data breach at $4.45 million. This is a figure from the 2023 report, not a current estimate specifically for Shadow AI incidents. It nevertheless gives an idea of the financial impact that data breaches can have on organisations.

Companies often hold information that gives them an advantage over competitors. It may include source code, product designs, pricing strategies, financial models, customer information or future business plans.

Keeping such information confidential is an important part of protecting trade secrets.

If employees regularly enter this material into public AI tools without checking the provider's terms or the organisation's security arrangements, the company may weaken its ability to show that it took reasonable steps to protect the information.

The legal position will depend on the relevant law and circumstances. But the business concern is simple: information that was meant to remain inside the organisation may be shared with an external service without proper control.

Blocking AI websites may appear to be the easiest response. A company can restrict access through its network, issue a policy and warn employees against using unapproved tools.

But consider the earlier example of the junior associate. Blocking a website on a company laptop does not prevent the associate from opening the same website on a personal phone. A personal hotspot can also take the activity outside the company's network.

The organisation may see that its office systems are following the policy. It may not see what is happening elsewhere.

This creates a difference between controlling access and controlling actual use.

A company that provides approved AI tools can set rules about who can use them, what information can be shared and which security measures apply. It can also review usage through appropriate technical controls.

By contrast, when employees use personal accounts and devices, the organisation may lose access to important information about that activity. It may not know which tools are being used, what information has been shared or whether an incident has taken place.

This does not mean companies should allow every AI tool. Some uses should remain prohibited, especially where sensitive information cannot be adequately protected. But treating a ban as the complete solution overlooks the reasons employees may continue using AI.

The issue is not simply whether an organisation permits or prohibits AI. It is whether its policy gives employees a safe and practical way to complete their work.

Companies need a system that protects information without ignoring the way employees actually work. This does not require unrestricted AI access. It requires clear rules, suitable tools and safeguards that match the sensitivity of the information.

1.⁠ ⁠Provide Approved Enterprise AI Tools

If employees are using public AI tools because they need help with everyday tasks, organisations should consider providing approved alternatives.

Enterprise AI services may offer different contractual and technical protections, including limits on data retention and commitments about whether customer inputs are used for model training. Some providers also offer Zero Data Retention (ZDR) arrangements.

The aim is to give employees a reliable tool for their daily work without making them depend on personal accounts or unapproved services.

2.⁠ ⁠Use Local AI Models for Highly Sensitive Information

Some work involves information that should not be sent to an external AI service. This may include sensitive source code, confidential legal strategy, certain client documents or important business information.

For such work, organisations can consider running AI models on their own infrastructure or within a controlled private environment.

Open-source model families such as Llama and Mistral may be considered for internal deployment, depending on the organisation's technical needs and resources. For particularly sensitive work, a disconnected or air-gapped system may offer an additional layer of protection.

But local deployment is not automatically safe. The organisation still needs to manage access, system security, updates and the information employees enter into the model.

3.⁠ ⁠Create a Clear Data Classification System

Employees should not have to guess whether a document can be shared with an AI tool. Organisations need to make these rules clear so that employees can understand what information is safe to share and what needs protection.

One practical way to do this is dividing information into three categories: public, internal and condidential.

Public information, such as published reports, press releases, and public case laws, can be used with apporved public or enterprise AI tools. Internal information, including routine meeting notes and general internal dragts, should only be used with AI tools approved under company policy. Confidential information, such as client records, personal data, contracts, source code and M&A information, requries greater care. Employees should use restricted tools or seek additional approval before sharing them.

This system should be easy to understand and connected to the organisation's existing confidentiality rules. Legal teams may need additional restrictions for privileged communications, litigation material and client documents.

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools can help organisations identify and control the sharing of sensitive information.

For example, these tools can detect personal indentification numbers, financial details or confidential information in data being sent to external AI services. Depending on how the system works, it may block the request, flag it for review or remove senstive information before it reaches an external service.

These tools are not perfect. They may miss information or flag material that is harmless. They should therefore support, rather than replace, clear policies and employee awareness.

Even a well-designed policy can fail if employees do not understand how to follow it in their daily work.

Organisations should explain which AI tools are approved, what information must not be shared, when human review is required and how employees can request access to a new tool.

They should also create a simple way for employees to report accidental disclosure. If people are afraid to report mistakes, organisations may learn about incidents too late to respond effectively.

At the same time, employees must remain responsible for following the rules. Practical alternatives do not remove the duty to protect confidential information. Organisations need both clear expectations and fair accountability.

Shadow AI is not going to disappear simply because an organisation blocks access to certain AI tools. Employees still have deadlines, daily tasks and work to complete. When approved tools are unavailable or difficult to use, some may look for other ways to get the same work done.

This creates a problem for organisations. They may have rules against using unapproved AI services, but those rules do not necessarily tell them where employees are actually using AI or what information they are sharing.

This does not mean employees should be free to use any tool they want. Confidential information still needs protection, and employees must take responsibility for how they use AI. But organisations also need to look at why employees are turning to tools outside the approved system.

If a tool is helping employees complete routine work more easily, the organisation should consider whether it can provide a safe alternative. It should also make clear what information can be shared and where approval is required.

The real issue is not just whether employees are following AI policies. It is whether those policies work in the way people actually do their jobs. If organisations want to manage Shadow AI, they need to understand its use rather than simply try to stop it.

#9590. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9588. Find resellers selling below your MAP price every day with Python

If you sell a product through other shops, you need to know which of them list it below your minimum advertised price (MAP), and you need to know it the day it happens, not at the end of the month.

This is part 3 of a small series. In part 1 I compared one product's price across stores, and in part 2 I added a change mode that returns only offers whose price or stock moved. This post adds the MAP check I built on top of it this week: give it your MAP and it flags every offer below it, with the gap in money and in percent. Real output from today (2026-11-14) is below, plus the limits.

A script helps, but then you own the scraper, the currency conversion, the per-product MAP table and the "what changed since yesterday" logic. That last part is the one that breaks.

I built the Cheapest Price Finder on Apify. You give it product page URLs from any stores. It reads the real price from each page's structured data (JSON-LD offers, Shopify product data, meta price tags), converts everything to one currency with daily ECB rates and sorts the offers from cheapest to most expensive.

Every row then gets mapPrice, belowMap (true/false), mapGap (how far below MAP, in money; negative means above MAP) and mapGapPercent. RUN_SUMMARY.mapCheck lists belowMapCount and belowMapUrls, so one key tells you whether today needs attention.

Create a free Apify account and copy your token from Console (Settings, API and Integrations):

For the demo I used the AeroPress Original at four coffee shops. I am not the brand and I do not know AeroPress's real MAP, so I picked a made-up MAP of $42, and for one store a separate MAP of $49.95 to show the per-URL override:

Note the Intelligentsia row: it is below MAP but out of stock. Whether that counts as a violation is your policy, so the tool reports availability and leaves the decision to you.

With onlyChanged, the first run returns every offer once as new. I ran it twice today with MAP $39.95 and the same monitorId:

So on a normal day your script prints nothing. On the day a reseller cuts the price, you get one row with changeType: "priceDrop", previousPrice, priceChange and the MAP gap together.

Or run the Python file from your own cron:

The MAP check (not the change mode) also works through plain HTTP APIs with one key:

I tested this path today too: the same two rows came back with belowMap true and false. onlyChanged and monitorId are switched off on these APIs on purpose: the remembered prices would live in my account and be shared by every caller with the same URLs. Keep yesterday's rows yourself there, or use the Apify actor for the built-in change feed.

On Apify it costs $3.00 per 1,000 saved results. With onlyChanged, unchanged offers are not saved and not billed, so 50 resellers checked daily cost nothing for results on a quiet day. Apify's free plan includes a small monthly credit, enough to try it. On API.market and radarbg.com there are free plans to test first.

I built this because MAP checks are the same price scrape plus one comparison, and the comparison is what people end up doing by hand. Now one field does it.

If you manage a brand with resellers, try it on Apify with 3 to 5 of your reseller pages. How many reseller pages would your daily list have? If a page returns "no price found", post the URL in the comments and I will look at it.

#9584. Which Model Should You Use? Frontier, Hosted or Local? It Depends.

This article provides a roadmap for choosing where to run a model: on your own machine, through a hosted API, on Cloud Run, or on an accelerator you rent. Every figure comes from a measured run in gemma4-dev, which serves Gemma 4 on more than a hundred hardware and engine combinations and now carries five Gemini API models as sibling rigs.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon arrived on the Gemini API next to 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash and Gemma 4. On 2026-11-14 all seven ran through the same Gemini API endpoint, started together, with the same GSM8K (1,319 math word problems) and BFCL simple (400 function calls) questions and scoring, with thinking set as low as each model accepts:

Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon are ahead of Gemma 4 31B on GSM8K, with the 95% range of the difference above zero, and level with it on BFCL. Output prices include thinking tokens, and thinking decides the bill. On Hydrogen and 3.8 Flash it cannot be turned off: Hydrogen has the lowest Gemini 4 price, thought on every problem at its lowest setting, and cost the most. It is also the fastest Gemini 4 model, about 2.7 times quicker per problem than Argon. The times come from all seven sharing one connection at once. Carbon and Argon double in price on 2026-12-01. The method is in the companion article, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Carbon and Argon Against Gemma 4.

Four ways to run a model, each measured in this repo:

The RTX 3050 serves Gemma 4 E2B on six engines. One request at a time without a drafter they run from 61.9 tok/s (LiteRT-LM) to 121.1 tok/s (vLLM); with Google's speculative-decoding drafter vLLM reaches 230.5 tok/s. Under load, with 64 requests at once of 128 tokens in and 512 out, SGLang delivers 1,711.3 tok/s in total and vLLM 1,651.2.

The same card holds the larger models one request at a time: 12B at 56.4 tok/s with its drafter, 26B A4B at 40.6 tok/s on code with its experts in system RAM, and 31B at 4.0 tok/s with two thirds of it on the CPU. Quality rises with size: GSM8K 0.9014 (E2B), 0.9629 (12B), 0.9735 (31B).

The 1650 Ti laptop card decodes E2B at 73.75 tok/s for one request and peaks at 164 tok/s through its server at 16 requests. The laptop CPU decodes 16.71 to 18.86 tok/s.

Setup: llama.cpp is ready 4 s after start, vLLM 48 s. vLLM's first start compiles for about 3.5 minutes. The hardware is already paid for, and nothing is billed per hour.

Gemini API. A key and an HTTP call. The Gemini models and Gemma 4 26B and 31B answer the OpenAI chat format at /v1beta/openai/chat/completions. Estimated from the token counts returned and list prices, a full 1,319-problem GSM8K run cost $0.87 on Flash-Lite, $1.66 on 3.8 Flash, $3.15 on Argon, $3.70 on Carbon and $4.51 on Hydrogen. Gemma 4 is on the free tier only, with paid use not available, and its free-tier rate limit answered three requests in the GSM8K and BFCL runs with HTTP 429 after every retry.

AMD Token Lab. Gemma 4 31B on an SGLang router on AMD GPUs, free with the AMD AI Developer Program: 10 points for 30 days, with Gemma 4 31B at 0.035 points per million input tokens and 0.07 per million output. One request at a time decoded at 2.0 to 7.6 tok/s on the shared service, with up to 5 s before the first token. The limit is 128 requests at once across all users; over that, the reply is HTTP 429.

One L4 GPU in us-east4 with 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM. Output rose with concurrency to 188.46 tok/s at 4 requests and stayed there at 8 (189.53), because the service was deployed with --concurrency=4; more users means more instances. The same L4 on EC2 reached 360.17 tok/s at 8.

At list price the instance costs $1.4209 an hour, which works out to $7.95 per million output tokens at one request and $2.08 at eight. Cloud Run scales to zero by default, so an idle service costs nothing and the next request waits for a cold GPU start; the startup check waits 180 s before its first look. The weights load from Cloud Storage.

TPU v5e, one chip. Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM: 143.9 tok/s for one request, 1,689.1 tok/s at 64 requests (128 in, 512 out), GSM8K 0.9007 and BFCL 0.920. Flex-start costs $0.60 per chip-hour, about $0.089 per million output tokens at full batching and $1.31 at one request. Capacity came within two to five minutes in us-west4-a, and the engine took 12.6 to 14.1 minutes to start on most rigs, most of it compiling (27.2 on one).

TPU v5e, four chips. E2B as four one-chip engines reaches 7,788 tok/s at 64 requests and 14,189 at 256. The 12B fits with 122,624 tokens of context cache, against 9,728 on one chip.

EC2 G6, one L4. vLLM at 132.8 to 140.4 tok/s for one request and 3,715.7 tok/s at 64; with the drafter, 4,516.3. A spot g6.2xlarge measured on an older vLLM cost $0.9412 an hour, $0.73 per million output tokens at eight requests.

AMD MI300X. 192 GB on one card: E2B at 340.4 tok/s for one request and 10,293.6 tok/s at 64 (128 tokens of context). $1.99 an hour, billed while powered off too: $0.054 per million output tokens at 64 clients and $1.624 for a single stream.

Every rented option above has two prices per million tokens, one at a single request and one at full batching: Cloud Run $7.95 and $2.08, TPU v5e $1.31 and $0.089, MI300X $1.624 and $0.054. A machine that serves one user at a time costs about what a hosted API charges, or more. A per-token API charges the same at any load.

Pick by the axis that matters most, then check the others.

By cost. Free first: your own card, Token Lab, and the Gemini free tier, which carries Gemma 4 26B and 31B, Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash and Hydrogen. For paid use with light or uneven traffic, pay per token: both tests cost $0.92 on Flash-Lite and $3.46 on Argon. Hydrogen thought on every request and 3.8 Flash on most; Google's docs say reasoning cannot be turned off on Gemini 3 or Gemini 4 models, and the API runs none as low. Compare models by cost per answer. From 2026-12-01, when Carbon and Argon go to $4 / $20, this run costs $6.93 on Argon and $5.02 on Hydrogen, by arithmetic from list prices. A rented machine wins only when it is kept busy, which brings TPU v5e to $0.089 and MI300X to $0.054 per million output tokens.

By speed. On a hosted API, Flash-Lite answered a GSM8K problem in 1.10 s and Hydrogen in 2.84 s; Gemma 4 on the Gemini API took 8 to 9 s. For one user, a local card with a drafter (230.5 tok/s on the 3050) or an MI300X (340.4). For many users, the MI300X or four TPU v5e chips. Cloud Run as deployed here stops at 189.53 tok/s per instance.

By accuracy. Gemini 4 Argon leads GSM8K at 0.9841, and Argon and Gemma 4 31B lead BFCL at 0.9675, on short problems with thinking at its lowest setting. For hard, multi-step work Google calls Carbon "our strongest frontier model"; that case was not measured here. Where a model runs did not change its score: Gemma 4 31B answered 1,284 of 1,319 GSM8K problems through the Gemini API and 1,284 on an RTX 3050 with llama.cpp, differing on 8 problems. Model size matters more than where it runs: E2B scored 0.8954 to 0.9030 on GSM8K across six engines on the RTX 3050, the L4 and TPU v5e, and the 31B 0.9735.

By ease of use. A hosted API needs a key. A local card needs a driver and an engine, and llama.cpp is ready in seconds. Cloud Run needs a container and a deploy and then scales on its own. A rented accelerator needs capacity, a 12.6 to 14.1 minute engine start on TPU, and someone to turn it off.

The goal of this article was to map where each way of running a model fits. The key to the solution was a single repo that measures local cards, hosted APIs, Cloud Run and rented accelerators with the same engines, scoring script and questions. The results were:

Scope: figures come from separate runs between 2026-09-03 and 2026-11-14 in gemma4-dev, on different engine versions and days; each is quoted from its run's report, and ratios between runs on different hardware are indicative. Prices are list prices on the date each run recorded them. Accuracy was measured on GSM8K and BFCL simple only, and not on Cloud Run, Token Lab or the MI300X; the throughput figures are Gemma 4 E2B unless a size is named. Gemini API throughput under load was not measured.

The strategy for choosing where to run Gemma 4 and Gemini was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

#9583. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

 

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.


The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.


Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Automatically Mint Your Content As NFTs



Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.


Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.


Alternatively, LimeWire acknowledges the importance of exclusivity. Creators can choose to share their posts exclusively with their premium subscribers. In doing so, the content remains a special offering solely for dedicated fans, creating an intimate and personalized experience within the LimeWire community. This flexibility in sharing options emphasizes LimeWire's commitment to empowering creators with choices in how they connect with their audience and distribute their digital creations.


After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.


If you make it public, anyone can discover your content and even trade the NFTs. If you choose to share the post only with your premium subscribers, it will be exclusive only to your fans.


Earn Revenue From Your Content

Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other users who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.


This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.


LMWR Tokens

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

Pricing Plans

You can sign up to LimeWire to use its AI tools for free. You will receive 10 credits to use and generate up to 20 AI images per day. You will also receive 50% of the ad revenue share. However, you will get more benefits with premium plans.

  • Basic plan: 

For $9.99 per month, you will get 1,000 credits per month, up to 2 ,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 50% ad revenue share

  • Advanced plan: 

For $29 per month, you will get 3750 credits per month, up to 7500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 60% ad revenue share

  • Pro plan: 

For $49 per month, you will get 5,000 credits per month, up to 10,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

  • Pro Plus plan: 

For $99 per month, you will get 11,250 credits per month, up to 2 2,500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share

With all premium plans, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.

Sign Up Now To Get Free Credits

Conclusion

In conclusion, LimeWire emerges as a democratizing force in the creative landscape, providing an inclusive platform where anyone can unleash their artistic potential and effortlessly share their work. With the integration of AI, LimeWire eliminates traditional barriers, empowering designers, musicians, and artists to publish their creations and earn revenue with just a few clicks.


The ongoing commitment of LimeWire to innovation is evident in its plans to enhance generative AI tools with new features and models. The upcoming expansion to include music and video generation tools holds the promise of unlocking even more possibilities for creators. It sparks anticipation about the diverse and innovative ways in which artists will leverage these tools to produce and publish their own unique creations.


For those eager to explore, LimeWire's AI tools are readily accessible for free, providing an opportunity to experiment and delve into the world of generative art. As LimeWire continues to evolve, creators are encouraged to stay tuned for the launch of its forthcoming AI music and video generation tools, promising a future brimming with creative potential and endless artistic exploration

#9582. Crypto: Balancing Potential and Limitations – What Problems Can Digital Currencies Actually Solve?

The most enthusiastic crypto supporters once claimed (and some still do) that digital currencies can address all the flaws, risks, gaps, and shortcomings that burden the traditional financial system and that so many people are dissatisfied with. Except the reality has demonstrated they quite obviously can’t.

Crypto is indeed an exciting and promising innovation that has already proven it can be useful in many real-life situations, but that doesn’t automatically turn it into a fix-it-all. It’s not able to substitute fiat, nor can it single-handedly address issues like economic inequalities, structural inflation, security risks, and other similar problems.

However, if crypto were completely useless, we wouldn’t still be talking or hearing about it so often – but we are. If you want to know how far digital currencies have come and what’s happening in the crypto space at the moment, you can check out the Top Cryptocurrency News Today | Binance Square and read about the latest events and developments in the industry.

So, if crypto can’t bring world peace, what exactly can it do, and how far do its powers extend?

People were initially reluctant to engage with crypto and didn’t know what to make of it, but once the fear of the unknown subsided and curiosity took over, they realized that digital currencies possess certain qualities that can make them useful in various circumstances, as follows.

Diversification is a must in investment in order to reduce the risk of losses, and it relies on a simple principle of spreading capital across various types of assets with different risk profiles instead of concentrating it in a single one. Over the years, crypto has grown into quite a popular investment tool, even though it was intended to serve as a payment solution. Long story short, digital currencies have found their way into many investors’ holdings, and some of them have earned substantial profits from their crypto investments.

A portfolio can be well-balanced even if it doesn’t contain a single crypto, so digital assets aren’t a requirement for diversification. But the fact that they have a relatively low correlation to traditional markets, being driven by a different combination of factors, and can bring in outsized gains due to their sharp price swings makes them a good choice in this respect. Nevertheless, experts recommend keeping crypto allocations low (between 1% and 5% of a total portfolio) to protect against volatility risks.

Crypto is powered by blockchain technology, which means issuance and transactions are managed by a network of nodes instead of a single central entity, like governments, banks, and payment processors. This unique structure gives crypto the possibility to help with economic mobility.

By removing the intermediaries, coins can be transferred directly from one person to another, so the funds can arrive in the recipient’s wallet almost instantly, whereas with fiat, it can take up to several days for transactions to be processed, especially for international transfers that involve more cumbersome bureaucratic procedures.

Transaction speed is not the only aspect that crypto can improve, but affordability as well. Because there are no middlemen to incur processing fees, transferring crypto is cheaper than transferring conventional currencies.

And let’s not forget about all the people in the world who can’t use banking services because of all the barriers they impose. Crypto is easily accessible to everyone as long as they have a smart device and internet connection.

Another advantage that derives from crypto’s decentralized architecture is the ability to conceal users’ real identity. Crypto wallets are pseudonymous, so holders are not required to share sensitive data like legal names and personal addresses in order to use crypto. The blockchain also offers a public record of all the transactions it has ever processed, giving everyone the possibility to verify transfers and offering a level of transparency that fiat money cannot match.

The advantages that crypto offers seem absolutely amazing, but volatility casts a shadow over all these perks. Digital currencies can be a good addition to investors’ holdings, as they can offer high growth, but if the allocations are not well balanced, a market downturn can drag the entire portfolio down.

At the same time, the alleged decentralization that removes intermediaries from the equation and makes crypto transactions faster and cheaper in theory doesn’t always apply in practice. In many situations, crypto transactions run through centralized exchanges, or the projects are controlled by a foundation or corporate entity, which goes against the decentralization ethos that digital assets promote. So, instead of offering a different path to transferring value than traditional finance, crypto often uses the same centralized mechanism.

Using crypto to pay for goods and services is not practical because, once again, volatility gets in the way. With crypto values shifting constantly, it’s extremely challenging for companies that accept crypto payments to price their products and protect their profits. Many resort to payment processors to help them deal with volatility, but that kind of contradicts the whole idea of embracing crypto to bypass the middlemen.

It’s bold, if not downright absurd, to say that crypto can provide the answer to all of society’s money-related problems. But it’s equally absurd to dismiss it as a useless tool when it’s already being used in so many areas, and its integration into global finance continues to grow. Digital currencies can step in instances and areas where conventional banking services are either absent or highly inefficient. The takeaway here is that they can only serve as a complementary solution, not a complete replacement for traditional financial systems.

Financial Advice Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Cryptocurrency investments carry significant risks, and readers should conduct their own research before making financial decisions.

#9581. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9579. The tampered Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace: what teams should check

Posted on Nov 14 • Originally published at reclaimllm.com

Cursor's notice on tampered Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313: who was exposed, how to check a machine, and extension controls to add.

On October 29, 2026, tampered copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension were served from Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace for about 11 hours. Cursor's security notice provides indicators of compromise and cleanup scripts; its fuller incident update is dated November 13.

This post summarizes what the official sources say, how a team can check its machines, and which extension controls to add. Everything about the malware comes from Cursor's notice and two independent analyses. Where the sources do not say something, we do not guess.

Affected artifact. Anthropic.claude-code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS, installed or updated from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace (Cursor security notice).

Exposure window. About 2:27 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time on October 29, 2026 (about 5:27 a.m. to 4:35 p.m. in Toronto) (Cursor security notice).

Who published it. Not Anthropic. Cursor's update says an attacker used a credential stolen from Cursor's internal systems to place the tampered copies directly on the cache that serves Cursor's extension marketplace. Cursor says this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product, and that Open VSX, the marketplace source, never had the malware (Cursor incident update). Microsoft reports that the malicious packages were never published on the Visual Studio Marketplace or in the npm package @anthropic-ai/claude-code (Microsoft Security Blog). StepSecurity reports that Anthropic confirmed 2.1.313 was never published on any official channel and skipped to 2.1.314 to avoid confusion (StepSecurity).

How many people. Cursor says at most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions on October 29 potentially received the malicious build, and that it contacted affected customers directly (Cursor incident update).

How it started. Cursor's update traces the attack to an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, an inference vendor. The key was exposed at Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks. That data included some credentials, which the attacker used to reach other Cursor systems (Cursor incident update; Fireworks security bulletins).

Cursor's notice says the tampered extension:

Cursor also says that turning on the SSH service needs admin rights, which the extension does not have on most macOS and Windows hosts, so on those hosts the tunnel step failed. But the extension still added the key, installed persistence and sent host details. The attacker's server has been taken offline (Cursor security notice).

Microsoft's analysis adds two useful details. The loader sends environment variable names, not values. And the code runs when the extension module loads, so no Claude conversation is needed (Microsoft Security Blog). StepSecurity's analysis agrees that loading the module is enough (StepSecurity).

A version number alone does not prove compromise. StepSecurity notes that the 2.1.312 build on Open VSX is a different, clean file. What matters is the source (Cursor's marketplace), the platform (macOS or Windows) and the time (the October 29 window).

List exposed machines. Use your endpoint or extension-installation telemetry to find Cursor installs that installed or auto-updated Anthropic.claude-code to 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 during the window. Check whether Cursor or your team admins received a notice from Cursor.

Check each candidate machine for the SSH key. Cursor's notice gives a one-line check for macOS and a PowerShell check for Windows. Both look for svc-telemetry in the authorized keys files. Copy the commands from the notice, not from a third-party page.

Hunt for the published indicators. A missing SSH marker alone does not rule out exposure; correlate installation records, process activity and persistence artifacts. The notice lists file hashes, the attacker IP, persistence file paths, the scheduled task name and the SSH command line. Microsoft publishes Defender hunting queries for the same indicators.

Cursor's notice gives these steps for affected hosts (Cursor security notice):

Microsoft adds: preserve evidence (the extension package, modified SSH files, scripts and startup entries) before cleanup, and keep unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development settings (Microsoft Security Blog).

Questions go to security@cursor.com, the contact both Cursor posts give.

Users in the Cursor forum asked whether they can trust plugin updates (t/176923). Trust is a policy question. These controls reduce how much you depend on it.

Cursor documents these controls in its enterprise hardening guidance. Check the linked configuration pages for your client version and deployment method; do not assume every plan supports the same fleet-wide enforcement.

Use endpoint and extension-installation telemetry to investigate this incident. A captured AI session is not evidence that an extension was installed, and this article makes no claim that ReclaimLLM detected or blocked the tampered package.

What it does: it captures AI coding sessions from Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and Antigravity through hooks, and makes them searchable. After an incident like this, that record can help answer a narrower question: during the exposure window, which sensitive values appeared in the captured agent sessions on an affected machine. That is supplementary evidence: it cannot establish every credential the compromised host could access or narrow the vendor's rotation guidance. Detection of secrets and external egress in captured sessions runs on an hourly or daily sweep and raises alerts; it does not block.

For the broader agent setup, see our Claude Code security guide.

Cursor says no: Anthropic did not publish the tampered copy, and it was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product (Cursor incident update). Microsoft says Anthropic confirmed its systems were not compromised.

According to Cursor, Microsoft and StepSecurity, the tampered builds were only served from Cursor's marketplace. The Visual Studio Marketplace, Open VSX and the npm package were not affected.

Cursor's notice names Windows and macOS builds. The indicator list also includes Linux file paths for the persistence scripts. Those artifacts do not establish that a malicious Linux package was distributed. If your Linux telemetry shows matching indicators, investigate them under your incident-response process.

Not by itself. The payload installs scripts outside the extension folder. Follow Cursor's cleanup steps.

#9576. Reusing Browser Profiles: A Subtle Automation Gotcha

Reusing browser profiles across automation runs seems efficient—until it quietly breaks your tests.

Browser profiles aren't designed for infinite reuse. Extensions update silently, storage bloats, and state leaks between runs. Worse, these issues manifest sporadically—making debugging a nightmare.

The fix is simple: rotate profiles or reset state between runs. Use fresh directories for each session, clear storage programmatically, or isolate with incognito modes. Treat profiles as disposable infrastructure, not persistent workspaces.

One clean profile per run eliminates an entire class of flaky tests.

#9571. Google Play Closed Testing Explained: The 14-Day Requirement & 12 Testers

Posted on Nov 14 • Originally published at 12testerhive.com

If you're an Android developer publishing on Google Play in 2026, you've probably hit the biggest wall for indie devs: Google's mandatory 14-day closed testing requirement.

For all personal developer accounts created after November 2023, Google requires a minimum of 12 testers opted into a closed testing track, actively testing your app continuously for 14 consecutive days before you can request access to the Production track.

I run 12TesterHive — we pair Google Play developers with verified Android testers every day — so this guide comes from daily hands-on practice, not theory. Here's the full roadmap: understanding the policy, configuring your testing tracks correctly, managing testers, and passing Google's production review with documented evidence.

Before this policy, anyone could pay the $25 registration fee and immediately upload an app to production. That led to:

The 14-day testing period forces real debugging and real user feedback — and it's an effective barrier against automated spam.

Most developers fail not because they didn't test, but because they misconfigured the Play Console.

In Play Console, select your app → Testing → Closed testing → Create track. Name it (e.g., "Alpha Testing").

In your closed track → Create new release → upload your AAB file → add release notes → Save → submit for review. The closed track must be approved by Google before testers can opt in (typically 1–3 business days).

⚠️ Testers must click the web opt-in link and hit "Become a Tester" BEFORE downloading the app — otherwise their participation won't register.

The rule says at least 12 testers. Recruiting exactly 12 is a recipe for failure, because people are human:

If you run with exactly 12 and one tester misses day 13, your 14-day timer can reset to zero.

This is why professional platforms (including ours) always run a +3 backup margin — 15 testers instead of 12 — so a single dropout doesn't cost you two weeks.

The most common misconception: "I'll have friends download the app once and leave it idle." That gets campaigns rejected. Google's automated review verifies sincere testing activity:

At 12TesterHive we validate this through a dedicated companion app, 12 testers — 12testerhive, which verifies device telemetry, blocks emulators/VMs, and logs daily active usage.

After day 14, the Play Console shows Apply for Production. Google reviews your answers manually — vague answers get rejected. How to handle each section:

Be specific. Not "It's a utility app." Instead: "My app is a personal budget manager for freelance developers to track daily expenses and export PDF tax reports."

Describe your methodology honestly. Example: "Testers were recruited through the 12TesterHive network — verified Android developers testing on physical devices across multiple regions."

Never write "Everything was perfect." Google knows every new app has bugs. Instead: "In the first 5 days, testers on Android 14 reported a rendering bug on the settings screen; I shipped v1.0.4 to fix it. Testers also requested dark mode, which I added in v1.0.5."

Does the timer reset if I release an update? No — updates during testing are recommended. They show you're actively responding to feedback.

Can I use emulators or bots? No. Google checks device fingerprints. Emulators, scripts, and VMs get flagged immediately — rejection or account termination.

What if my production request is rejected? Google gives feedback (usually "insincere testing"). Address it, run another closed test, and reapply.

Passing the 14-day closed testing requirement is about three things: correct console configuration, a safety margin of testers, and genuine daily engagement documented for the review. Nail those, and day 14 becomes a formality.

This is the full guide from our blog — originally published at 12testerhive.com (canonical source). If you're preparing your own closed test and have questions about the questionnaire or tester setup, ask away in the comments!
